articles.title: Under 25? Here's what the Budget means for you
articles.summary: The chancellor announced a series of measures which will impact under-25 year-olds from housing to minimum wage.
articles.content:
The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus.

The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the £450,000 cap.

The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.

The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.

The government had already revealed a £4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladder

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".
articles.reasoning: The article describes government measures aimed at helping under-25s access affordable housing through new savings accounts and financial support schemes. These policies have a broad and meaningful impact on young people struggling to enter the housing market, addressing a significant social issue with clear, detailed plans.
articles.personality_title: New Budget plans help under-25s save for their first home
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many young people under 25 find it hard to save enough money to buy their first home. The government wants to make it easier for them to get on the housing ladder.

**What happened** – The chancellor announced new Budget measures including a savings account called the "First Time Buyer Isa." Starting in 2029, this account will let savers put in up to £4,000 each year, and the government will add a 25% bonus to their savings. This replaces the current Lifetime Isa, which had strict rules and penalties. The new account will reduce penalties if money is withdrawn for reasons other than buying a home. Additionally, a housing scheme called "Your First Home" will help 70,000 first-time buyers in England by allowing them to buy new homes with just a 2.5% deposit and a government loan covering 20% of the property's price.

**Impact** – These plans make it easier and less risky for young people to save money for a house. The government’s loan helps lower the upfront cost of buying a home, especially for those without family support. This can help more young people, including couples, to afford their first home in both London and other parts of England.

**What's next step** – The new savings account will start in 2029, replacing the Lifetime Isa. Meanwhile, the "Your First Home" scheme is already planned to help thousands of buyers. The government will likely continue adjusting these programs to make home buying more affordable for young people.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New government savings accounts and loan programs will help under-25s save money and buy their first homes with less financial stress.

articles.title: Ending conflict is ‘number one thing’ to reduce world hunger, new WFP chief says
articles.summary: Reducing conflict is the single most effective way to tackle global hunger, the new head of the UN World Food Programme (WFP), Luke Lindberg, said on Wednesday, noting that conflict drives two thirds of the acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide.
articles.content:
“Conflict is a man-made situation. It is something that we can solve,” Mr. Lindberg told journalists at UN Headquarters in New York in his first press conference since taking office earlier this week.

“The number one thing we can do to reduce hunger in the world is to reduce the amount of conflict that is happening all around the world.”

Tweet URL

On top of that, El Niño is set to push 49 million more people into acute food insecurity, while chokepoints in global supply chains are exacerbating the problem further, he said.

‘Big platitudes’

Mr. Lindberg said WFP did not need “big platitudes or big announcements” but execution, built on three priorities: protecting staff, strengthening donor partnerships and improving operations “a little bit better each and every day”.

More than 700 humanitarians have been killed in the last few years while trying to save lives, he said. “Nobody should lose their life trying to save somebody else’s.”

He also pledged to keep investing in preparedness ahead of disasters, including through tools such as artificial intelligence, and to “go big” on school meals.

First trip to Sudan

Mr. Lindberg said his first trip as Executive Director would be to Sudan in a couple of weeks, to thank frontline staff working in “the most challenging places on Earth”.

Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia are the three operations where WFP is currently focusing, he said. “In the short run, it’s no more famines.”

Asked about Gaza, he said the number of people going hungry there was unacceptable, adding that while WFP has access to deliver food, it is cutting back because of funding shortfalls.

He pledged to stand up for WFP employees wherever they are located. “If anywhere in the world there are people attacking humanitarians, I will absolutely do what I can to protect them,” he said.

‘All-of-the-above approach’

On funding, Mr. Lindberg said the United States remains WFP’s largest funder, while the private sector is now its fifth-largest donor. “There is no one nation, no one entity that can do this alone,” he said.

Asked whether he saw himself as Washington’s representative at the UN, Mr. Lindberg called it “an unfair characterization”, saying his mandate from the Secretary-General is to end hunger and that he would be a “team player” across the UN system.

Mr. Lindberg said US President Donald Trump had personally called him to ask him to be the US nominee for the post, and that he had “a great relationship” with many members of the Trump administration.

People “all the way up the chain to the president” within the US Government want to support humanitarian work around the world, he said, adding that WFP also needs to build deeper donor partnerships with other countries.

Mr. Lindberg succeeds Cindy McCain, who led WFP from April 2023 to May 2026, and Carl Skau, who has served as Acting Executive Director since June.

The new WFP chief previously served as Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs with the US Department of Agriculture.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant and actionable approach to reducing global hunger by addressing conflict, which drives most acute food insecurity worldwide. articles.title: Ofcom sets out social media age-checking methods ahead of ban
articles.summary: Ofcom says photo and digital ID, banking checks or facial age estimation can help prove someone is 16 or over.
articles.content:
Ofcom has set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

Under the UK's social media ban - which is due to come into force in March next year - those under that age will be prevented from accessing ten of the biggest platforms, including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

Many UK adults are also likely to have to confirm that they are not under-age by using one of the proposed measures, which are subject to government approval.

A similar ban was introduced in Australia last year but many children there have found ways to get round it. The UK says it intends to take a tougher approach.

Age verification below 18 is challenging because 16 and 17 year olds don't have credit cards or full driving licences, and may not have passports either. They can also look significantly older or younger than they are.

To address that challenge, Ofcom has - in addition to traditional forms of ID - recommended four methods that it says would be "highly effective" at gauging people's ages:

photo ID matching, where relevant information on a photo ID document such as a passport is checked against a live image taken during an age check

banking-based checks, which involves using the information a financial institution has on record regarding a user's age

face age estimation technology (which the regulator argues has recently improved)

digital ID services, which enable people to digitally prove who they are or provide information about themselves, such as their age

The BBC has asked three of the UK's biggest banks whether they would have a process for assisting with social media requests for age verification if it did become an official measure.

However, ultimately it will be up to the tech companies to figure out how to implement the checks: the onus is on social network providers to come up with their own solutions and comply.

Ofcom CEO Dame Melanie Dawes said the regulator was drawing on its experience in introducing tougher age checks for porn sites last year:

"What we've learned in introducing age checks across the porn industry is that actually what a lot of countries did before us was say you need to do it this way and they were very prescriptive and it didn't work," she told the BBC.

"So what we've said all along is here are things that can work, they must preserve privacy, they must protect people's data, but it's on you to put in place what you think works for you."
articles.reasoning: The article reports on Ofcom's recommendations for effective age verification methods to enforce a social media age ban protecting minors under 16. This has broad societal impact by aiming to safeguard children from potentially harmful online content, representing a meaningful policy step with significant positive implications for child online safety and digital rights. The article provides detailed context on the methods proposed and the challenges involved, showing substance and a focused topic.
articles.personality_title: Ofcom proposes new ways to check ages for social media users under 16
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The UK plans to stop people under 16 from using popular social media sites like Instagram and TikTok starting next March. To do this, companies need ways to check users’ ages accurately.

**What happened** – Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, shared ideas on how to check if someone is 16 or older. They suggested using photo ID matching, bank records, face age estimation technology, and digital ID services. These methods aim to prove a user’s age while keeping their data safe.

**Impact** – This is important because checking ages on social media is hard, especially for 16- and 17-year-olds who may not have usual ID like passports or credit cards. Ofcom’s recommendations offer clear options to help stop younger children from seeing content meant for older users, protecting their safety online.

**What's next step** – The government still needs to approve these ideas. After that, social media companies will decide how to use these age checks on their platforms. Ofcom will keep making sure the rules work and protect people’s privacy.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Ofcom has outlined practical ways to verify ages on social media, aiming to keep under-16 users safe by enforcing the upcoming age ban in the UK.
articles.personality_title_fr: Ofcom propose de nouvelles méthodes pour vérifier l'âge des utilisateurs de moins de 16 ans sur les réseaux sociaux
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Royaume-Uni prévoit d'empêcher les moins de 16 ans d'utiliser des réseaux sociaux populaires comme Instagram et TikTok à partir de mars prochain. Pour cela, les entreprises doivent trouver des moyens fiables de vérifier l'âge des utilisateurs.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Ofcom, le régulateur britannique des communications, a proposé des méthodes pour vérifier si une personne a 16 ans ou plus. Il s'agit notamment de la correspondance avec une pièce d'identité, des contrôles bancaires, de la technologie d'estimation de l'âge par le visage et des services d'identité numérique. Ces méthodes visent à prouver l'âge tout en protégeant les données personnelles.

**Impact** – Cela est important car vérifier l'âge sur les réseaux sociaux est difficile, notamment pour les 16-17 ans qui n'ont pas toujours de pièces d'identité classiques comme le passeport ou la carte bancaire. Les recommandations d'Ofcom offrent des solutions claires pour empêcher les plus jeunes d'accéder à des contenus réservés aux plus âgés, assurant leur sécurité en ligne.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement doit encore valider ces propositions. Ensuite, les plateformes sociales décideront comment appliquer ces contrôles d'âge. Ofcom continuera de superviser pour garantir le respect des règles et la protection de la vie privée.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Ofcom a présenté des méthodes concrètes pour vérifier l'âge sur les réseaux sociaux, afin de protéger les moins de 16 ans grâce à l'interdiction prochaine au Royaume-Uni.

articles.personality_presentation_es:
